subtype: Signalling a turn in group discussion [Regulating]
passage: Seminar note, Thursday. Parul, a second-year student, sat at the far corner of the table during today's discussion on urban housing. When the argument turned to rent controls, Parul lifted one finger just off the table, leaned forward a little and caught my eye as chair. I nodded that I'd seen it and let the speaker finish. Two others talked over each other while Parul waited, hand still raised, jaw set. When the speaker paused I said, "Parul, go ahead." The point was clear and changed the direction of the talk. Afterwards Parul said the waiting was hard. I told Parul the signal was noticed and I'd keep a list of turns. I'll say that to the whole group next week.

qa.q: Which topic was the seminar discussing?
qa.a: The seminar was discussing urban housing, turning to rent controls.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling while waiting with a raised finger?
qa.a: Parul wanted to contribute and was likely tense or impatient, as the set jaw and the raised hand suggest. Another reading is that Parul was simply keen to make sure the point was not lost.

qa.q: What could the chair do to help quiet students claim a turn?
qa.a: Keep a visible list of turns and tell the whole group that raised fingers and leaning in are being noticed.

qa.q: How might the two who talked over each other see Parul's waiting?
qa.a: They may not have noticed the signal at all, or may have seen it and felt rushed, so a chair's clear turn order helps them too.

grounding: A young adult signals a turn by lifting a finger, leaning in and catching the chair's eye, and patient signalling gains influence.

subtype: Signalling a turn in group discussion [Regulating]
passage: Tuesday night, Naveen writing. Seminar today and I finally got a word in. I've been the person who blurts, so Suraj, the chair this week, had warned me last time. Today I tried something different. When Ananya started on the water policy paper, my hand went up a few inches, I leaned forward, and I tried to catch Suraj's eye. My heart was thumping and my foot kept jiggling because I wanted to jump in right then. I didn't. I counted two speakers. Then Suraj nodded at me and I said my bit, short. Priya said afterwards that it landed better than usual. I feel calmer than I expected, and a bit proud. 🙂

qa.q: Who was the chair this week?
qa.a: Suraj was the chair this week.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling while waiting to speak?
qa.a: Naveen was eager and nervous, shown by the thumping heart and jiggling foot, and wanted to jump in at once. Holding back also shows Naveen cared about not interrupting again.

qa.q: What small step helped Naveen get a turn?
qa.a: Naveen raised a hand a few inches, leaned forward, caught the chair's eye and waited for two speakers before talking.

qa.q: How might Suraj have seen Naveen's behaviour this time compared with before?
qa.a: Suraj had warned Naveen about blurting, so waiting to be nodded at probably looked like better turn reading and more respect for others.

grounding: A young adult claims a turn with a lifted hand, a lean in and eye contact, and waits patiently instead of interrupting.
